sentences.text: Suzhousaurus was an unusually large therizinosauroid that grew to a length of six meters and a mass of nearly three point one tonnes.
Unlike later relatives, its backbones were not filled with air spaces, yet the hip structure showed a distinct backward curve typical of the group.
Scientists identify this animal by a rounded top edge on the hip bone, a wide opening in the pelvic bone, a short thigh bone with a deep notch, and a rear leg bone that curves backward.
Researchers located two specimens during fieldwork campaigns in the years 1999 and 2004 within the Xiagou and Zhonggou rock layers.
The primary specimen, cataloged as FRDC-GSJB-99, was unearthed in the Yujingzi Basin inside the Xinminbao Group.
A team led by Li Daqing formally named the genus Suzhousaurus and the species S. megatherioides in the year 2007.
The name Suzhousaurus honors Suzhou, which was the historical name for the Jiuquan region where the fossils were found.
Suzhousaurus functioned as a relatively large herbivore within its ancient environment.
Evidence from related dinosaurs suggests this animal possessed at least some feathers, a trait supported by impressions found on other therizinosauroids.
The right upper arm bone measured fifty-five centimeters and lacked a prominent bump found in other species, while the thigh bone was thickened and robust at eighty-four centimeters long.
In its original description, the genus was placed in the Therizinosauroidea superfamily in a basal position.
Later studies in 2019 classified it as a therizinosaurid, though often as a close relative to the Therizinosauridae family with weak statistical backing.
This creature lived approximately 115 million years ago during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous period in Asia.
The older specimen dates to the early to middle Aptian from grey rock layers, while the younger one comes from red beds of the early Albian.
At that time, a large lake bordered by narrow hills likely existed in the area, helping dinosaur groups move through the landscape.

Some researchers propose that Suzhousaurus might be the same animal as the earlier therizinosauroid Nanshiungosaurus bohlini, but a direct comparison is difficult because the original specimen of N. bohlini is missing and the available bones do not overlap.
